title: Transposing Sketchpad
user: Beginning composers writing for transposing instruments who need to hear and enter the sounding pitch without repeatedly doing notation arithmetic.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A programmer asking how to start composing explicitly weighs theory, an instrument, and software for tinkering with sounds.
MuseScore reports that computer-keyboard note entry does not honor the selected sounding pitch for a Bb clarinet, a concrete transposition friction.

recurrence: Two independent music-making contexts in 2025: a novice asks where to begin, while notation users report an unresolved sounding-vs-written-pitch workflow break. It interrupts every note, not just export.
current_workaround: Use a piano roll with no notation context, calculate transpositions by hand, or enter written pitch in a full notation editor and repeatedly check playback.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore, Flat, and DAWs can transpose, but they begin as complete notation or production environments. None makes a tiny instrument-aware sketch surface whose default interaction teaches what the player hears versus reads.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a two-staff written/sounding view, six common transposing instruments, keyboard/MIDI entry, instant playback, and a shareable eight-bar sketch. Non-goals: full score engraving, cloud collaboration, sample libraries, or AI composition.
success_measure: In a 20-user beginner test, 70% can enter and correctly explain an eight-bar Bb-clarinet melody after one session, with no external transposition reference.
monetization: free — a frictionless, no-account learning tool is more useful before a user has committed to a music package.
constraints: Web MIDI must remain optional; audio and files stay local by default; use only freely licensed synthesized sounds and clear instrument-range warnings.
why_distinct: It treats transposition as an audible learning interaction rather than a hidden setting in a notation suite.

title: MIDI Roundtrip Check
user: Electronic musicians and score arrangers who need to know whether an exported MIDI file preserves the pitch bends, channels, and controller intent they heard while composing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A prospective electronic-music learner says there is no clear documentation for getting started and asks for the first composing steps.
A MuseScore request details missing General MIDI port/channel controls and inaccurate exports including breath control, program changes, and guitar pitch bends.

recurrence: A 2026 beginner thread and a detailed, active notation-export request point to a repeatable handoff failure between the friendly composing surface and downstream hardware/DAWs.
current_workaround: Import the file into another DAW, listen track by track, inspect raw MIDI events, or keep an old version of the notation app for export.
incumbents_and_gap: MIDI-OX, DAW event lists, and MuseScore diagnostics expose low-level events, but none produces an approachable before/after report tied to a reference render and General MIDI expectations.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop utility that opens a MIDI file, visualizes channel/program/controller timelines, flags likely unsupported or out-of-range events, and exports a concise sharing report. Non-goals: MIDI editing, sequencing, audio generation, or hardware driver installation.
success_measure: For a fixture set containing missing pitch bends, wrong channels, and dropped controllers, the utility identifies at least 90% of seeded discrepancies and explains each without raw-byte inspection.
monetization: one-time — export verification is episodic, and creators should be able to run it offline around their own files.
constraints: Parse malformed MIDI defensively; never upload compositions; label heuristics as warnings rather than making playback-correctness guarantees.
why_distinct: It is a creative-file fidelity receipt, not another DAW or notation editor.

title: Flipbook Proof
user: Illustrators and teachers turning a short video into a physical flipbook who need a printable, traceable frame plan before spending days drawing pages.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creator asks how to produce hand-drawn flipbook-style animation from video and outlines a manual ffmpeg, pose-estimation, line-art workflow.
A feature request asks for laser strokes that remain visible until manually cleared, because transient marks disappear before a presenter can use them.

recurrence: Both requests center on temporal visual guidance that vanishes too quickly: one needs stable frames for drawing, another needs a persistent visual trace. The cost is wasted hand-drawing time.
current_workaround: Extract frames with ffmpeg, arrange them manually in a design app, use onion-skin software, or pause a video and trace with no page-order or exposure guidance.
incumbents_and_gap: EbSynth, Krita, and full animation packages offer parts of the workflow, but they do not make a browser-local print proof with selected frames, onion-skin overlays, page numbers, and binding-safe margins.
smallest_useful_product: Client-side web app that ingests a local short clip, lets the user choose frame count and crop, shows adjacent-frame onion skin, and prints numbered trace sheets with a thumbnail contact sheet. Non-goals: AI rotoscoping, video hosting, style transfer, or social sharing.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot users print a complete 24-page proof and report no page-order or binding-margin mistake in their first physical flipbook.
monetization: one-time — it has a tangible project outcome and handles private source video locally.
constraints: Process video in-browser where feasible; cap clip duration on low-memory devices; do not include copyrighted example footage or claim automated artistic authorship.
why_distinct: The deliverable is a practical physical-production proof, not a generic video filter or animation editor.

title: Lesson Motion Cues
user: Teachers and technical educators who want cartoon-like explainer animations controlled by code but need a readable cue timeline rather than an animation engine project.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An educator likes Scratch's sound and art capabilities but explicitly asks for a more cartoon-like animation library controllable through an API.
A Godot proposal says animation start/end ranges require manual scripting; interrupted animations can leave a corrupted state.

recurrence: The education ask and the engine-level timing proposal identify the same boundary: authors can draw scenes, but coding reliable time spans and cues is onerous.
current_workaround: Script timers in a game engine, use Scratch manually, or edit keyframes in professional animation software and lose a code-readable lesson representation.
incumbents_and_gap: Manim is code-first but not cartoon-oriented; Scratch is approachable but not API-driven; Godot is capable but carries engine setup and timing semantics. A small cue-oriented layer is missing.
smallest_useful_product: A browser canvas with named actors, a timeline of enter/move/say/highlight ranges, JavaScript data export, and self-contained SVG/MP4 render. Non-goals: character rigging, AI video generation, full game-engine export, or hosted classrooms.
success_measure: An educator can make and export a 45-second narrated concept animation with three timed actors in under 30 minutes, and its JSON can be regenerated deterministically.
monetization: freemium — a free local editor proves the workflow; optional hosted lesson templates can support maintenance.
constraints: Accessibility needs captions and reduced-motion previews; use user-owned SVG/audio only; make the generated timeline portable and versioned.
why_distinct: It is a cue sheet that happens to render, bridging educator intent and code rather than duplicating Scratch or Manim.

title: Animatic Event Strip
user: Solo 2D animators and small game teams who need to plan visual beats, sound cues, and interaction windows before committing to a full animation package or engine scene.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creator directly asks whether any tools can create simple 2D cartoon animation.
Godot users request animation markers decoupled from target methods because current call tracks bind an animation to implementation details.

recurrence: The simple-animation request and game-engine marker request converge on a low-friction planning need: define beats independently before code and assets harden around them.
current_workaround: Use sticky notes and a video editor, put placeholder code calls directly in an engine animation, or maintain a spreadsheet that drifts from the animatic.
incumbents_and_gap: Storyboarder and video editors plan shots; Godot and Unity execute events. They do not offer a tiny, engine-neutral strip where frames, voice clips, and semantic markers are one portable artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Offline timeline with image cards, waveform snippets, named markers, frame-range labels, and JSON/CSV export for Godot/Unity adapters. Non-goals: tweening, character animation, AI image generation, or a full project manager.
success_measure: A five-person pilot can turn a 30-second scene into a marker list with fewer than one ambiguous implementation question per scene during handoff.
monetization: one-time — it is a focused creative-planning utility whose file portability matters more than an account.
constraints: Keep media local by default; adapters must be clearly versioned; do not bundle fonts, clips, or character assets without suitable licenses.
why_distinct: The core unit is an implementation-neutral event strip, not an AI animator or replacement game engine.

title: Life Lab Notebook
user: Students, families, and creative coders exploring cellular automata who need to compare rules and preserve surprising discoveries without learning a programming environment first.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN thread seeking the best Conway's Game of Life implementation attracts 47 comments and points to continuous variants with emergent creatures.
A Godot proposal says simulation and life-sim games repeatedly need their own time/calendar model and asks for a built-in abstraction.

recurrence: A lively implementation-comparison thread and a separate simulation-time request show enduring interest in experimentation, but the learning loop is split across code, engine configuration, and screenshots.
current_workaround: Open one-off web demos, modify source code, take screenshots, or build a bespoke simulation clock in a game engine.
incumbents_and_gap: Golly, Lenia demos, and engine tutorials are powerful but either scientific, code-centric, or isolated. They lack a kid-friendly experiment notebook that records rule, seed, time scale, and outcome side by side.
smallest_useful_product: Static web lab with Life-like and continuous presets, adjustable clock/season modifiers, side-by-side rule comparison, named snapshots, and a single-file experiment export. Non-goals: online leaderboards, crypto collectibles, arbitrary code execution, or AI discovery claims.
success_measure: In classroom testing, 75% of pairs can reproduce a peer's saved experiment and explain which rule/time change produced a different outcome.
monetization: free — a linkable exploratory simulation is most valuable when students can use it without accounts or payment.
constraints: Bound grid and simulation work to protect browsers; distinguish illustrative models from scientific simulations; ensure keyboard controls and colorblind-safe states.
why_distinct: It turns cellular automata from a one-off visual toy into a reproducible, social learning record.

title: Inclusive Game Jam Cards
user: An adult and child making a first tiny browser game together who need a playful path from paper mechanics to an accessible playable prototype in one sitting.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An adult asks for the best stack to make a simple game with an 11-year-old in a weekend and wants visual joy in a few hours; replies recommend paper mockups and tiny HTML games.
A screen-reader user describes the Godot editor as so cluttered that reaching a selected node's properties requires tabbing across many unrelated regions.

recurrence: The family game-making request and accessibility report point to the same exclusion: heavyweight editors create too much setup and navigation before the first fun interaction.
current_workaround: Start in Scratch/Godot, follow a tutorial, or use paper and then have the adult translate the idea into code.
incumbents_and_gap: Scratch is broad and valuable; Bitsy is constrained; Godot is powerful. None starts with co-designed mechanic cards that generate a deliberately tiny, keyboard-accessible web game skeleton.
smallest_useful_product: A browser card deck for goal, control, obstacle, feedback, and accessibility choices that produces a one-screen HTML game template plus a printable playtest sheet. Non-goals: AI code generation, account-based classrooms, asset marketplace, or general game engine.
success_measure: In 10 observed adult-child sessions, eight pairs reach a playable keyboard-only game and complete one paper playtest within 90 minutes.
monetization: free — the point is a low-barrier first creative experience; paid printable educator packs could be considered only after validated use.
constraints: No child accounts or telemetry; generated games must work without external assets; follow WCAG keyboard, contrast, and reduced-motion basics.
why_distinct: It begins with game-design conversation and inclusive constraints, not an empty editor or an LLM prompt.

title: Daily Range Puzzle
user: Friends who want a free, browser-based daily puzzle with a small cooperative tactical layer rather than another solitary word game.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user explicitly seeks additional free web games with one new puzzle each day, mostly beyond their current word-game list.
A dedicated wargaming/TTRPG group asks for a shared ruler because map distance needs to be fixed and visible to every viewer.

recurrence: A direct daily-web-game request and a separate tabletop group's measurement need suggest an underserved overlap: light daily puzzles that reward discussing a shared board and distances.
current_workaround: Play individual word puzzles, use virtual tabletops built for longer campaigns, or share screenshots and estimate ranges verbally.
incumbents_and_gap: Wordle-style sites solve solo daily novelty; Roll20 and Foundry serve full tabletop campaigns. Neither offers a 3-minute, no-login, shared-distance daily micro-puzzle.
smallest_useful_product: Static daily seeded hex-board puzzle with fixed map scale, one cooperative link, keyboard/touch controls, and a spoiler-safe results card. Non-goals: chat, user-generated campaigns, gambling mechanics, ads, or account streak pressure.
success_measure: At least 35% of completed games are opened by a second participant via the share link, while median first-session completion stays under five minutes.
monetization: free — daily web games compete on instant access; a voluntary tip page is less distorting than streak-driven monetization.
constraints: Use deterministic public seeds with no personal data; make color-independent terrain markers; avoid copyrighted game rules and names; provide offline replay of prior days.
why_distinct: It uses distance as the shared reasoning mechanic, not as a thin reskin of a word puzzle or virtual tabletop.

title: Score-Aligned Choir Cleanup
user: Community choirs preserving archival recordings when they have the score but need a cautious, local way to make rehearsal copies easier to hear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A choir archivist asks for tools to improve poor SATB recordings, separate parts, reduce noise, and ideally use the exact score as guidance.
Audacity's open issue requests grouping audio clips with labels, showing continuing need to keep editorial audio fragments meaningfully organized.

recurrence: The direct score-aware restoration request and a contemporary audio-editing organization request both expose the gap between a raw recording timeline and the musical structure people actually need to work from.
current_workaround: Try generic denoisers, manually cut and label sections in Audacity, pay a restoration engineer, or accept an archive that is hard to rehearse from.
incumbents_and_gap: iZotope RX and Audacity offer powerful generic cleanup; source-separation services offer automated stems. None makes a conservative score/section-aligned rehearsal copy workflow for volunteer ensembles without uploading heritage recordings.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop app that imports audio plus a MusicXML/PDF section map, lets the user mark rehearsal passages, applies transparent local noise/EQ presets, and exports labeled excerpts with an edit receipt. Non-goals: voice cloning, generative replacement vocals, automatic perfect source separation, or cloud storage.
success_measure: Five pilot choirs can produce a labeled rehearsal pack for one archival piece in under an hour, and 80% of singers rate section intelligibility higher than the original.
monetization: one-time — preservation groups need local, durable tooling and cannot justify recurring per-minute processing fees.
constraints: Keep recordings local; require rights confirmation before export; preserve originals and make every filter reversible; do not promise forensic restoration or individual-part isolation.
why_distinct: It connects careful restoration to rehearsal structure instead of pretending a generic AI enhancer can recreate a lost performance.

title: Sound Pattern Playground
user: Students and hobbyists experimenting with their microphone who need to understand what an on-device sound classifier notices before training or embedding one.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A developer asks for local/on-device sound models that recognize patterns such as laughter, crying, and emotions, and asks where to begin.
A Godot user requests a frequency-response graph because dB descriptions alone do not make an audio filter's effect understandable or precise.

recurrence: Both threads ask for interpretable audio feedback rather than a black box: one wants local pattern recognition, the other cannot reason about an audio setting without visualization.
current_workaround: Copy a pretrained model demo, inspect librosa notebooks, or adjust EQ/filter controls by ear with no connection to features or classifier confidence.
incumbents_and_gap: Teachable Machine, librosa, and DAW analyzers each cover a piece, but none combines privacy-preserving microphone capture, visibly explained features, and a tiny local label experiment focused on learning.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that records short user-consented clips, shows waveform/spectrogram/MFCC-like features, collects three labels, runs a transparent in-browser nearest-neighbor baseline, and exports the dataset. Non-goals: emotion inference, surveillance, cloud training, or medical/safety classification.
success_measure: In a workshop, 80% of participants can collect three classes, explain one visible feature difference, and identify one misclassification in 25 minutes.
monetization: free — education and privacy are strongest with a no-account local tool; paid curriculum material is possible later.
constraints: Never label people or infer sensitive traits; get explicit mic permission; store clips locally and make deletion obvious; disclose that simple features are illustrative, not diagnostic.
why_distinct: It teaches the sensory evidence behind a classifier instead of wrapping an opaque audio AI API.

title: Generative Palette A11y
user: Generative-coding artists publishing interactive sketches who need palettes that retain their intended mood while remaining distinguishable to more viewers.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN participant seeks photography and generative-coding artists, books, websites, and projects as creative reference material; the thread drew 51 comments.
p5.js tracks feature work around its accessibility color-naming support, evidence that color interpretation remains an active concern in a core creative-coding ecosystem.

recurrence: A substantial generative-art discovery discussion and active accessibility-color work in p5.js indicate a broad creative audience that needs color feedback inside, not after, the sketching process.
current_workaround: Use a generic contrast checker after choosing colors, guess at colorblind simulation, or sacrifice a palette's relationships to satisfy a single pass/fail score.
incumbents_and_gap: Coolors, Adobe Color, and contrast checkers are palette tools; p5.js offers accessibility descriptions. They do not evaluate a time-varying generative palette against the actual proportions and motion of a sketch.
smallest_useful_product: Browser tool that accepts a palette plus a small canvas preview or frame sequence, simulates common color-vision differences, reports confusable regions, and proposes bounded lightness/chroma alternatives while preserving hue relationships. Non-goals: AI art generation, universal accessibility certification, or hosting artists' work.
success_measure: On a corpus of 30 generative sketches, users retain at least 80% of their original palette swatches while removing the top reported confusable pairing in 70% of revisions.
monetization: free — broad adoption benefits an open creative-coding ecosystem; a paid batch/export API can follow only if demand exists.
constraints: Frame analysis stays local; describe simulations as approximations; avoid treating color vision as a monolith; publish any palette metric and conversion assumptions.
why_distinct: It checks the visual behavior of generative work, not just isolated swatches or an AI-generated image.

title: Local Sketch Deck
user: Creative learners who miss HyperCard's draw-and-script immediacy and need to make small interactive cards locally without being pushed into a full web framework.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A creator asks for a modern HyperCard successor, citing the cost of LiveCode, Decker's visual limits, Scratch's game focus, and the lack of an integrated graphical environment in toolkit languages.
An Excalidraw issue documents Ctrl+S accidentally invoking browser Save As instead of reliably saving the creative document when text is being edited.

recurrence: The successor request lists multiple rejected tools, while a browser-canvas save failure underscores that local-file ownership and frictionless persistence remain foundational creative needs.
current_workaround: Use Decker/LiveCode, assemble HTML/CSS/JS by hand, repurpose Scratch, or draw mockups in one app and code interaction in another.
incumbents_and_gap: Decker is deliberately retro; Scratch is game-led; web IDEs are code-led; Excalidraw is drawing-led. There is room for a current, offline-first card canvas with a tiny explicit behavior vocabulary.
smallest_useful_product: Desktop app with cards, editable text/buttons/images, five inspectable actions (show, hide, change text, play sound, go to card), local project files, and static HTML export. Non-goals: arbitrary plugin code, cloud sync, app-store packaging, collaboration, or AI app generation.
success_measure: In a first-use study, 70% of participants create a three-card interactive story, save it locally, reopen it, and export a working HTML version within 45 minutes.
monetization: one-time — a personal creativity environment should remain useful as a local file format without ongoing hosting charges.
constraints: Projects must be ordinary, versionable files; sandbox exported behaviors; include keyboard navigation and accessible text semantics; never silently overwrite a project.
why_distinct: It restores an integrated draw-plus-behavior learning surface with deliberately bounded interactions, rather than imitating a full programming language or app builder.
